bodies.subtitle: Launch pads, flight centres and tracking stations
bodies.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic (latitude, longitude east of Greenwich)
bodies.coordNote: Coordinates are the surveyed centres of launch pads, buildings and antennas. Launch facilities are tiny compared with a planetary globe, so markers on Earth are best explored after zooming in.
bodies.intro: Every journey off this planet started somewhere on it — a concrete pad in Florida, a test stand in Mississippi, a control room in Texas, an antenna dish pointed at the Moon.

bodies.name: The Moon
bodies.subtitle: Six crewed landings, five Surveyors, Soviet landers and every crater we made

bodies.intro: Twelve people walked here. Dozens of machines arrived and never left. Impact scars, abandoned descent stages and mirrors still reflecting laser light from Earth.

bodies.name: Mars
bodies.subtitle: Landers, rovers and the wreckage of everything that missed
bodies.coordSystem: IAU 2015 planetocentric areographic coordinates, east longitude
bodies.coordNote: Landing coordinates are the published fixes (NASA Mars24 lander catalogue for NASA missions, with the reference papers cited per record). On a global view markers can be many kilometres wide — treat them as site markers, not pinpoint footpads.
bodies.intro: Seven working landers, four dead rovers, and a handful of spacecraft that hit the ground harder than intended. Each one is still exactly where it stopped.

bodies.name: Venus
bodies.subtitle: Four probes that reached the surface and stopped transmitting
bodies.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric Venus coordinates, east longitude
bodies.coordNote: Venus is permanently cloud-covered. Coordinates are the entry-point fixes published by NSSDCA for the Pioneer Venus probes; the exact landfall of each crushed probe is known only to a few tens of kilometres.
bodies.intro: Nobody has ever seen Venus from the ground. Four NASA probes fell through the clouds in 1978; one kept radioing for 67 minutes after impact.

sites.name: Langley Research Center
sites.mission: Viking project management, Lunar Orbiter, Mercury
sites.categoryDetail: Research centre — early human spaceflight and Mars landers
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Campus centre point.
sites.summary: America's oldest aeronautics laboratory, which managed the Viking landers and tested the Mercury capsule.
narrative: Langley was established in 1917 as an aeronautical laboratory and became the birthplace of American human spaceflight: the Mercury capsule was designed and tested here, and the original seven astronauts trained partly in its facilities. Its engineers ran the wind tunnel and flight tests that decided what a spacecraft should look like.

Langley also managed the Lunar Orbiter programme, which photographed 99% of the Moon and produced the maps Apollo used, and the Viking project, which put two landers on Mars in 1976 — the first successful landing on another planet. Viking's biology experiments and its images of a rust-coloured plain transformed the public idea of Mars.

The centre is still active in aeronautics, atmospheric science and planetary instrument development. Its headquarters building dates from the 1920s, and the centre's wind tunnels include some of the oldest large-scale facilities in the world still in use.

sites.name: Jet Propulsion Laboratory
sites.mission: Ranger, Surveyor, Voyager, Mars rovers, and many more
sites.program: NASA field centre (FFRDC managed by Caltech)
sites.categoryDetail: Laboratory and mission control
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Main campus centre point.
sites.summary: A graduate student project that turned into the place where America's robotic spacecraft are built and flown.
narrative: JPL began in 1936 with a group of Caltech students testing rocket motors in the Arroyo Seco. During the Second World War it became an Army facility; in 1958 it was transferred to the new civilian space agency, and it has managed NASA's planetary programmes ever since.

Every US spacecraft that has touched another world was largely designed, built or operated here: the Rangers that photographed the Moon before crashing into it, the Surveyors that landed, the Mariners, the Voyagers, the Vikings, the rovers from Sojourner to Perseverance. The laboratory also runs the Deep Space Network's operations, and its mission control rooms are the places where signals from spacecraft billions of kilometres away are received.

The campus is a working laboratory rather than a museum. Its buildings include the Space Flight Operations Facility, still in daily use; the nearby Arroyo Seco, where the first rockets were tested, is now a hiking trail with a small plaque.

sites.name: Ames Research Center
sites.mission: LCROSS, Kepler, Pioneer, lunar mission support
sites.categoryDetail: Research centre — lunar and planetary science
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Campus centre point.
sites.summary: A wind-tunnel laboratory that became the home of NASA's lunar impactor and the search for other Earths.
narrative: Ames was founded in 1939 as an aeronautical laboratory and grew into a centre for space science, supercomputing and astrobiology. Its wind tunnels tested the shapes of Mercury capsules and the Space Shuttle; its life scientists ran the experiments that asked whether biology could survive on other worlds.

Ames managed the LCROSS mission, which fired a Centaur stage into Cabeus crater in 2009 and found water in the plume. It also ran the Kepler space telescope, which discovered thousands of exoplanets, and the Lunar Prospector mission that first detected hydrogen at the lunar poles.

The centre sits beside Moffett Field, whose enormous Hangar One — built for airships in the 1930s — is one of the most recognisable structures in the Bay Area. The campus still works on lunar science, planetary protection and the design of instruments for future landers.

sites.name: White Sands Missile Range
sites.mission: V-2 tests, Space Shuttle landing site, Apollo-era testing
sites.categoryDetail: Test range and emergency Shuttle landing site
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Range headquarters area; the historic launch complexes are spread across the range.
sites.summary: Where captured V-2s were fired into the desert, and where one Space Shuttle landed on a gypsum flat.
narrative: In 1946 captured German V-2 rockets were assembled and fired from White Sands, carrying instruments to the edge of space. Those flights produced the first photographs of Earth from high altitude and some of the earliest data on the upper atmosphere, and they established the practice of launching scientific payloads on military rockets.

The range's most unusual spaceflight connection is a landing: on 30 March 1982 Space Shuttle Columbia touched down on Northrup Strip at White Sands, the only Shuttle landing in the continental United States outside Florida. The site had been prepared as a backup runway, and high winds in Florida forced its only operational use; the gypsum dust that coated the orbiter caused problems for weeks afterwards.

The range is still active, and the Trinity Site, where the first nuclear device was tested in 1945, lies within its boundary. Its landscape of white dunes and black lava is used to this day for testing instruments that will operate on other planets.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: New Mexico, between Las Cruces and Alamogordo

sites.name: Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex
sites.categoryDetail: Deep Space Network antenna complex
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Complex centre point; individual antennas are within a few kilometres.
sites.summary: A cluster of dishes in the Mojave that has been listening to spacecraft since the first American lunar probes.
narrative: Goldstone began as a single 26 m antenna in 1958, built to track the Pioneer lunar probes. It grew into one of the three complexes of NASA's Deep Space Network, alongside Madrid and Canberra, positioned roughly 120° apart so that at least one can see any spacecraft at any time.

The 70 m DSS-14 antenna, completed in 1966, was built for the Apollo programme and later upgraded. It is the largest fully steerable antenna in the network and has tracked Voyager 1 and 2 into interstellar space, received data from every Mars surface mission, and performed radar observations of near-Earth asteroids.

The complex is in the desert for a reason: radio quiet. Its dishes are now surrounded by the Mojave National Preserve, and the site operates a visitor centre with one of the antennas — a 34 m dish — open for tours.

sites.name: Goddard Space Flight Center
sites.mission: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, NSSDCA, Explorer missions
sites.categoryDetail: Space science centre and national data archive
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Campus centre point.
sites.summary: Home of the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and of the archive this archive depends on.
narrative: Goddard was NASA's first space flight centre, established in 1959, and it has managed an extraordinary fraction of the agency's scientific spacecraft. It runs the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, whose cameras produced the coordinates used throughout this archive, and it hosts the National Space Science Data Center (NSSDCA) and the Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, where mission records, images and instrument data are preserved.

The centre also built and operates the networks that talk to spacecraft: the Near Earth Network and the Space Network are coordinated from Greenbelt, and the Deep Space Network's operations are shared with JPL.

The NSSDCA pages documenting lunar landing sites and anthropogenic impacts were written and maintained here by Dr. David R. Williams. Without that catalogue, an archive of abandoned spacecraft would have to start from scratch; with it, every marker on the Moon in this application can be traced to a specific table with a specific author.

sites.name: Marshall Space Flight Center
sites.mission: Saturn V, Lunar Roving Vehicle, Hubble Space Telescope
sites.categoryDetail: Propulsion and payload development centre
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Campus centre point.
sites.summary: The centre that developed the Saturn V, built the lunar rover, and later managed the Hubble Space Telescope.
narrative: Marshall Space Flight Center was established in 1960 around Wernher von Braun's rocket team, which had been developing ballistic missiles for the US Army at Redstone Arsenal. Its first great project was the Saturn family: the Saturn I, Saturn IB and Saturn V launch vehicles, developed and tested mostly in Huntsville and at the Mississippi Test Facility downriver.

After Apollo, Marshall built the Lunar Roving Vehicle — a contract that produced three flight vehicles and changed what crews could do on the surface. The centre also developed the Shuttle's solid rocket boosters and external tank, managed the Hubble Space Telescope, and now leads the Space Launch System.

The centre's test stands and the Saturn V display at the adjacent US Space & Rocket Center make it one of the few places where the full scale of the Moon rocket can be seen at ground level — a complete Saturn V lying on its side in a hall built around it.

facts.label: Key projects
facts.value: Saturn I/IB/V, Lunar Roving Vehicle, Shuttle boosters, Hubble, SLS

sites.name: Launch Complex 5 — Mercury-Redstone
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — first American crewed spaceflights
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Centre of launch complex 5, adjacent to pad 6.
sites.summary: The small concrete pad where Alan Shepard became the first American in space, seven weeks after Gagarin.
narrative: Complex 5 was built for the Redstone, a medium-range missile adapted to carry a Mercury capsule on a ballistic trajectory. On 5 May 1961 Freedom 7 lifted off with Alan Shepard aboard, flew 187 km downrange and splashed into the Atlantic 15 minutes later. It was not an orbit, but it was the flight that started American human spaceflight.

On 21 July 1961 Gus Grissom flew Liberty Bell 7 from the same pad. His capsule sank after splashdown when the hatch blew, and Grissom nearly drowned. He later commanded the first Gemini crewed flight and died in the Apollo 1 fire at pad 34, 4.5 km away along the same coastline.

The pad is preserved, with its blockhouse and the concrete ramp that carried the rocket to the launch mount. It is one of the few places where the physical scale of the first American space programme can be seen: the Redstone was 25 m tall, and the whole complex could fit inside the flame trench at pad 39A.

sites.name: Michoud Assembly Facility
sites.mission: Saturn V first stages, Shuttle external tanks, SLS core stage
sites.categoryDetail: Large-scale manufacturing plant
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Plant centre point.
sites.summary: Where the first stage of every Saturn V was welded together, and where Shuttle tanks and SLS core stages were built.
narrative: Michoud is a former war-time shipyard east of New Orleans with some of the largest manufacturing buildings in the world. NASA took it over in 1961 to build the Saturn V's first stage, the S-IC: 42 m long, 10 m in diameter, with five F-1 engines and a thrust of 34 meganewtons.

Thirteen S-IC stages were built and flown. After Apollo the plant switched to the Space Shuttle external tank, producing 136 of them, and then to the core stage of the Space Launch System. In 2018 the plant was in the path of Hurricane Katrina's successors and has been rebuilt several times; the tooling, cranes and vertical assembly cells are still in use.

Michoud is the kind of place that never appears in a launch highlight reel, but every Saturn V that went to the Moon began here, as sheets of aluminium alloy welded in a building long enough to hide a rocket inside.

sites.name: Johnson Space Center — Mission Control
sites.mission: Gemini, Apollo, Skylab, Space Shuttle, ISS
sites.categoryDetail: Crewed spaceflight centre and historic mission control room
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Main campus centre point; the historic Mission Control room (Building 30) is on the south side.
sites.summary: The room where every Apollo landing was flown, and where the phrase Houston, we've had a problem was first heard.
narrative: The Manned Spacecraft Center opened in Houston in 1961, on land donated by Rice University, and was renamed for Lyndon Johnson in 1973. Its Flight Control Room 2 — now a National Historic Landmark — was the operational heart of the Apollo programme: the room where flight directors Gene Kranz, Chris Kraft and their teams made the decisions that determined whether a crew came home.

On 13 April 1970 Apollo 13's oxygen tank exploded while the spacecraft was 330,000 km from Earth. The room's response — powering down the command module, using the Lunar Module as a lifeboat, and improvising a carbon-dioxide scrubber from plastic bags and cardboard — is one of the more remarkable feats of engineering management in the 20th century.

Mission Control still operates the International Space Station from the same building complex. The historic room has been restored to its Apollo-era appearance, down to the consoles, the flight director's loop and the ashtrays. Tours of Johnson Space Center include the room, and it is one of the few places where the physical workplace of space exploration has been preserved.

sites.name: Launch Complex 14 — Mercury-Atlas
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — orbital Mercury flights
sites.status: Decommissioned — pad preserved as a memorial
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Centre of launch complex 14.
sites.summary: The pad from which John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth.
narrative: Complex 14 launched all four orbital Mercury missions. On 20 February 1962 Friendship 7 lifted off with John Glenn aboard and completed three orbits, restoring American confidence after the Soviet flights of Gagarin and Titov. Scott Carpenter, Wally Schirra and Gordon Cooper followed from the same pad.

Mercury-Atlas was a difficult combination: a converted intercontinental ballistic missile as a crew launcher, with the astronaut in a capsule barely big enough to sit in. Two of the four missions had significant malfunctions — Carpenter's fuel and attitude problems, Cooper's failure of the automatic control system, which he flew by hand.

The pad was deactivated in 1966. In 1997 a group of Mercury veterans restored part of the complex, and a memorial stands near the original blockhouse and the base of the red gantry that once held Friendship 7.

sites.name: Launch Complex 19 — Gemini crewed launches
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — all ten crewed Gemini flights
sites.status: Decommissioned — pad and erector legs remain
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Centre of launch complex 19.
sites.summary: The most reliably crewed pad in American history: ten launches, ten crews, no failures.
narrative: Between March 1965 and November 1966 every crewed Gemini mission left from pad 19 on a Titan II. The pad had a distinctive white erector that held the rocket horizontally, lifted it upright with the crew already aboard, and swung away at ignition. The two astronauts rode to the pad standing in the white room and then sat in the capsule while it was raised.

Gemini is where the techniques for Apollo were worked out: rendezvous and docking, spacewalks, multi-day flights, and the experience of flying a spacecraft rather than simply riding in it. All ten crewed flights launched successfully, a record no other pad in the world has matched for crewed vehicles.

The pad was deactivated in 1967 when Apollo moved to the much larger Saturn IB and Saturn V complexes. The hardstand and the twin rails of the erector are still visible among the scrub at Cape Canaveral.

sites.name: Stennis Space Center test stands
sites.mission: Saturn V stage testing, Shuttle main engine testing, SLS
sites.categoryDetail: Rocket propulsion test facility
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Facility centre point; individual test stands are within a few kilometres.
sites.summary: The stand where every Saturn V first stage was fired before it was allowed near a launch pad.
narrative: Stennis, originally the Mississippi Test Facility, was built in the 1960s on a large tract of swamp and pine forest north of New Orleans. Its test stands were designed for the acoustic and physical violence of firing a Saturn V first stage on the ground: the B-1 and B-2 stands can hold a complete S-IC stage while all five F-1 engines run.

Every flight Saturn V first stage was acceptance-tested here, as were the second stages. After Apollo the site tested Space Shuttle main engines — more than two million seconds of firing over three decades — and now tests the core stage of the Space Launch System.

The test stands are surrounded by a buffer of more than 50,000 hectares, which has become a wildlife refuge. Alligators and bald eagles live inside the perimeter of a facility built to make the loudest machines in the world.

facts.label: Saturn V testing
facts.value: All flight S-IC first stages acceptance-fired

sites.name: Vehicle Assembly Building
sites.mission: Saturn V, Space Shuttle, Space Launch System
sites.categoryDetail: Vertical assembly building
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Centre of the building footprint.
sites.summary: One of the largest buildings in the world, built to stack Moon rockets indoors and still used to assemble rockets today.
narrative: The Vehicle Assembly Building is 160 m tall, 218 m long and encloses 3.7 million cubic metres — large enough that it has its own weather, and that the American flag painted on its side is 64 m wide. It was built so that a complete Saturn V could be stacked vertically indoors, out of the Florida rain, before being carried to the pad on a crawler.

Four high bays held the Apollo rockets; the same building was later converted for the Space Shuttle, with platforms and a lifting frame built around the orbiter and its external tank. After the Shuttle era it was modified again for the Space Launch System, whose core stage and boosters were assembled in the same high bay.

Its most distinctive feature is practical: the huge doors take 45 minutes to open, and the building's air conditioning is sized to keep the interior from condensing on a rocket's cryogenic tanks. The VAB is still the place where American heavy-lift rockets are put together, and it is visible from most of the Space Coast.

sites.name: Launch Complex 34 — Apollo 1 memorial
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — site of the Apollo 1 fire, later Apollo 7
sites.status: Decommissioned — concrete pad preserved as a memorial
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Centre of the remaining pad 34 hardstand.
sites.summary: Where three astronauts died in a fire on the launch pad, and where the first Apollo crew later flew in their memory.
narrative: On 27 January 1967, during a plugs-out test of the Apollo 1 spacecraft at pad 34, a fire broke out in the pure-oxygen cabin. Virgil Grissom, Edward White and Roger Chaffee died within seconds. The spacecraft had a hatch that could not be opened quickly against internal pressure, and the accident forced a complete redesign of the command module.

Pad 34 was rebuilt and, on 11 October 1968, launched Apollo 7 — the first crewed Apollo flight, and the mission that validated the redesigned spacecraft in Earth orbit. After Apollo 7 the pad was used for a few Saturn IB flights and then abandoned.

What remains is a concrete pedestal with the service structure legs cut off, standing in the Florida scrub. A plaque near the pad reads: In memory of those who made the ultimate sacrifice so others could reach for the stars. The launch complex is on the National Register of Historic Places; the gantry is gone, but the pad's four legs are still bolted to the concrete.

sites.name: Launch Complex 39A
sites.siteName: Kennedy Space Center, Merritt Island, Florida
sites.mission: Apollo, Skylab, Space Shuttle, commercial crews
sites.categoryDetail: Heavy-lift launch pad — Saturn V, Shuttle, Falcon 9
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Centre of pad 39A. The flame trench and hardstand are visible in satellite imagery.
sites.summary: The pad that sent humans to the Moon, then flew the Shuttle for 30 years, then became a commercial launch site.
narrative: Pad 39A was built for the Saturn V and first fired on 9 November 1967 with the uncrewed Apollo 4, an all-up test of the Moon rocket that engineers had decided to fly before putting a crew on it. Apollo 8 left from here on the first crewed flight around the Moon, Apollo 11 left from here on the first landing, and the pad went on to serve most of the lunar programme.

After Apollo, 39A was rebuilt for the Space Shuttle: the launch tower was replaced, the Saturn-era swing arms removed, and the pad's service structure redesigned around an orbiter standing vertically on an external tank. From 1981 to 2011 it launched Space Shuttle missions including the Hubble Space Telescope deployments and most of the assembly flights for the International Space Station.

Its third career began in 2014, when SpaceX leased the pad and modified it for Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy — including the return of Crew Dragon launches from American soil in 2020. Very little of the Apollo-era surface hardware survives; the concrete and the flame trench do. A pad is the one place where you can stand on the footprint of the Saturn V and watch a completely different rocket leave for orbit.

sites.name: Launch Complex 39B
sites.siteName: Kennedy Space Center, Merritt Island, Florida
sites.categoryDetail: Heavy-lift launch pad — Saturn V, Shuttle, Space Launch System
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Centre of pad 39B, north of 39A.
sites.summary: The other Apollo Moon pad, later rebuilt for the Shuttle and then for the rocket that will return crews to the Moon.
narrative: Pad 39B flew the dress rehearsal for the first landing: Apollo 10, in May 1969, went to the Moon, separated its Lunar Module and descended to within 15 km of the surface before returning — everything except the landing itself. It then hosted three Skylab crews on Saturn IB rockets, using a smaller vehicle on a pad built for something much larger.

Like 39A it was converted for the Space Shuttle, and it carried missions that could not be flown from the other pad, including the 1986 return to flight. After the Shuttle retired, 39B was rebuilt again around the Space Launch System, with a new mobile launcher and a crew access arm.

On 16 November 2022 Artemis I lifted off from 39B, sending an uncrewed Orion capsule around the Moon and back. The pad that launched the dress rehearsal for Apollo 11 is now the pad for the programme intended to follow it.

sites.name: Parkes Observatory — the dish that carried Apollo 11
sites.categoryDetail: Radio telescope used for NASA mission support
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Centre of the 64 m dish at the Parkes Observatory.
sites.summary: The Australian dish that received most of the world's television pictures of the first Moon landing.
narrative: Parkes is a 64 m radio telescope in the sheep country of New South Wales, built in 1961. When Apollo 11 flew, NASA needed a large antenna in the southern hemisphere to receive the television signal from the lunar surface during the long Australian night, and Parkes was the biggest and best available.

On 21 July 1969 the dish caught the signal from the Lunar Module's camera and passed it to the tracking station network for distribution. The moment Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon was received by the smaller antenna at Honeysuckle Creek near Canberra, which had a better angle; a few minutes later the feed switched to Parkes, which carried most of the rest of the broadcast. The images the world remembers — the ghostly, high-contrast picture of a man on the Moon — came through these antennas.

Parkes is still a working observatory, used for pulsar timing, fast radio bursts and spacecraft tracking. The story of that night was made into the film The Dish, which is more accurate about the sheep than about the timing.

facts.label: Apollo 11 role
facts.value: Received and relayed most of the lunar surface television, 21 July 1969

facts.label: Still operating
facts.value: Yes — pulsars, fast radio bursts, spacecraft tracking

sites.name: Honeysuckle Creek Tracking Station
sites.siteName: Namadgi National Park, Australian Capital Territory
sites.categoryDetail: Tracking station — received the first steps on the Moon
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Site of the former station; the 26 m antenna was moved to Tidbinbilla in 1983.
sites.summary: A 26 m dish in the hills above Canberra that received the first human footsteps on the Moon.
narrative: Honeysuckle Creek was one of NASA's Manned Space Flight Network stations, built in the bush south of Canberra to support crewed missions in the southern hemisphere. On 21 July 1969 its 26 m antenna was pointed at the Moon as Armstrong came down the ladder, and it received the first television pictures — inverted and high-contrast, but recognisably a man.

After about eight minutes the feed was switched to the larger Parkes dish, which had a better view and signal. Honeysuckle Creek continued to support Apollo and later missions, including the Apollo-Soyuz flight, and closed in 1981. Its antenna was moved to the Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex at Tidbinbilla, where it was used for another two decades.

The site is now a grassy clearing in Namadgi National Park with a few concrete footings and a plaque — one of the quietest places in the history of space exploration, and one of the most consequential.

sites.name: Space Launch Complex 41
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — outer planets and Mars 2020
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Centre of pad 41.
sites.summary: Both Voyagers left from this pad, and so did the rover now caching samples on Mars.
narrative: Complex 41 was built for the Titan III-C and modified for the Titan IIIE/Centaur, the combination needed to throw heavy payloads onto escape trajectories. Voyager 2 launched from here on 20 August 1977; Voyager 1 followed on 5 September, on a faster trajectory that would carry it past Jupiter and Saturn and out of the solar system.

The pad was rebuilt in the 1990s for the Atlas V. From it left New Horizons to Pluto in 2006, the Juno orbiter to Jupiter in 2011, the OSIRIS-REx sample-return mission in 2016, and on 30 July 2020 the Mars 2020 mission carrying the Perseverance rover and Ingenuity helicopter.
Voyager 1 and Perseverance, launched from the same concrete 43 years apart, are now the most distant human object and the most sophisticated machine on another planet. Both are still working.

sites.name: Space Launch Complex 17 — the Mars pad
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.mission: Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, Mars Polar Lander
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — most Mars surface missions of 1996–2008
sites.coordSystem: WGS 84 geographic
sites.coordNote: Centres of pads 17A and 17B; the site was cleared in 2018.
sites.summary: One Delta II pad complex launched nearly every American spacecraft that landed on Mars between 1996 and 2008.
narrative: Pad 17A and its twin 17B opened in 1957 and spent most of their lives launching Delta rockets. Their most remarkable run came at the end of the Cold War: Mars Pathfinder left from 17A in December 1996, Mars Polar Lander from 17B in January 1999, and then both Mars Exploration Rovers in the summer of 2003 — Spirit from 17A, Opportunity from 17B, three weeks apart.

Phoenix left from 17A in August 2007, the last Mars mission to use the pad. The Delta II was retired soon afterwards, and the two towers were demolished in 2018; the concrete pads and their flame trenches remain.

The complex is a useful corrective to the idea that launch sites are monuments. Some of the most consequential pads in planetary exploration were built for a workhorse rocket, flew a handful of historic missions, and were then taken apart when the rocket went out of service.

facts.value: Mars Pathfinder (1996), Mars Polar Lander (1999), Spirit (2003), Opportunity (2003), Phoenix (2007)

sites.summary: A 1960s Titan pad that became the busiest commercial launch site in the world — after being destroyed and rebuilt.
narrative: Pad 40 opened in 1965 for Titan III launches and was used for military and planetary missions for four decades. SpaceX took it over in 2007 and flew its first Falcon 9 from it in June 2010.

On 1 September 2016 a Falcon 9 exploded during a static fire test, destroying the rocket, its AMOS-6 satellite payload and much of the pad. The company rebuilt the complex in less than a year and returned to flight from the same concrete in December 2017.

Since then 40 has launched cargo and crew Dragons, dozens of Starlink batches and planetary missions including the DART asteroid impactor. It is a rare example of a launch pad that has been both abandoned and revived — twice over, with the Titan and Falcon eras separated by a rebuild.

sites.summary: InSight left Earth from California — the first planetary launch ever made from the west coast of the United States.
narrative: Almost every NASA planetary mission has launched from Florida, where the Atlantic provides a safe range for the drop stages. InSight broke that pattern. On 5 May 2018 an Atlas V lifted off from Vandenberg's pad 3E, flying south over the Pacific, because the mission's polar trajectory to Mars required a westward launch azimuth.

The rocket also carried Mars Cube One, two small CubeSats that flew separately to Mars and relayed InSight's entry, descent and landing telemetry back to Earth in real time — the first interplanetary CubeSats and the first time a Mars landing had been watched live by a dedicated relay.

The pad itself dates from 1962 and has launched Thor, Delta II and Atlas V rockets. It is a reminder that the geography of spaceflight is not fixed: a mission can require a launch site, a trajectory and a range that nobody had used for that purpose before.

sites.name: Mars 2 lander crash site
sites.categoryDetail: Failed lander — crashed during descent
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Published position: about 45° S, 47° E in Hellas Planitia. Exact impact point unknown.
sites.summary: The first human object to reach the surface of Mars arrived as wreckage, five days before its twin landed successfully.
narrative: Mars 2 released its lander on 27 November 1971 during a global dust storm. The descent system failed and it struck the surface in Hellas Planitia at high speed, becoming — unintentionally — the first human-made object to reach Mars.

Its orbiter continued to operate for months, returning images and data, and it carried the same Prop-M rover concept as Mars 3. Between them, the two Mars landers mark the beginning of the surface exploration of another planet: one crater, and one 20-second transmission.

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: Descent system failure during a global dust storm

sites.name: Mars 3 lander
sites.categoryDetail: Lander — first soft landing on Mars, 20 seconds of data
sites.status: Landed successfully; transmissions ceased after about 20 seconds
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Published position from NASA GISS: about 45° S, 202° E = 158° W. The lander has not been identified on the surface.
sites.summary: The first spacecraft to land softly on Mars sent a single partial image and then went silent forever.
narrative: Mars 3 arrived during a planet-wide dust storm in December 1971. Its descent system worked: the lander reached the surface in Ptolemaeus Crater and began transmitting after four minutes. The signal lasted about 20 seconds and produced a partial image of grey nothing before stopping, and no further contact was ever made.

The most probable cause was damage from the dust storm, either during descent or from electrostatic discharge — the same conditions that may have destroyed Mars 2 a few days earlier. What is certain is that the first soft landing on Mars happened in 1971, four and a half years before Viking 1.

The lander is still there in Terra Sirenum, and its final position has never been confirmed from orbit. It carried a small rover, Prop-M, that would have walked on skis tethered to the lander; it was never deployed.

sites.name: Viking 1 Lander — Thomas Mutch Memorial Station
sites.categoryDetail: Stationary lander — first successful Mars landing
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Radio-tracking fix from the landed spacecraft (Kuchynka et al., 2014), published by NASA GISS. 312.05° E is the same point as 47.95° W.
sites.summary: The first spacecraft to land successfully on Mars, and the first to look for life there. It sat in Chryse Planitia for six years.
narrative: Viking 1 landed on 20 July 1976 — seven years to the day after Apollo 11 — at 22.27° N, 312.05° E in Chryse Planitia. Its first image arrived minutes later: a rock-strewn plain under a pink sky, with one of the lander's footpads in the frame. It was the first photograph taken from the surface of another planet.

The mission's central experiment was the search for life. Three biology instruments fed soil samples with nutrients and looked for signs of metabolism; a gas chromatograph-mass spectrometer analysed the atmosphere and soil. One experiment produced a positive result that was later explained by reactive soil chemistry, and the consensus has been that Viking found no evidence of life — but it defined how the question would be asked for the next five decades.

Viking 1 also carried a seismometer, a meteorology boom and two cameras, and it operated for 2,245 sols, more than six years, until a command error in 1982 silenced it. The lander still sits in Chryse Planitia with its dishes and sampling arm. Orbital images from Mars Global Surveyor and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter have identified its hardware — including, in 2006, the parachute and backshell that delivered it.

artifacts.note: Imaged from orbit by MGS and MRO.

sites.name: Viking 2 Lander — Gerald Soffen Memorial Station
sites.categoryDetail: Stationary lander — northern plains
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Radio-tracking fix (Kuchynka et al., 2014) as published by NASA GISS. Some NASA pages quote 47.6–48.0° N.
sites.summary: The second Viking landed further north, where frost forms on the rocks in winter, and operated for three and a half years.
narrative: Viking 2 landed at Utopia Planitia on 3 September 1976, about 6,460 km from its twin. The site is further north and lower, and the images it returned showed a rockier surface with a dust-covered crust, together with something Viking 1 never saw: water frost on the ground in winter.

Its seismometer was mounted on the lander deck rather than the surface and never worked properly, but its cameras and weather instruments operated until April 1980, when its batteries failed after the mission had long exceeded its design life. The lander was renamed the Gerald Soffen Memorial Station after Viking's project scientist.

Like Viking 1 it is still in place, and its backshell and parachute have been photographed from orbit. The two Viking sites, 40° apart in latitude, are the oldest surviving artefacts on the surface of Mars.

facts.label: Notable observation
facts.value: Water frost on the surface during winter

sites.name: Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner — Carl Sagan Memorial Station
sites.categoryDetail: Lander and first Mars rover
sites.status: Last contact 7 October 1997 — lander and rover remain
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Radio fix (Kuchynka et al., 2014), published by NASA GISS; 326.75° E = 33.25° W. The rover's final position is within about 100 m.
sites.summary: A lander that bounced onto Mars inside airbags and released the first rover ever to drive on another planet.
narrative: Mars Pathfinder arrived on 4 July 1997 with a technique never used before: instead of retrorockets, it entered the atmosphere inside a heat shield, deployed a parachute, and then dropped the last few metres wrapped in airbags that let it bounce and roll across Ares Vallis. It came to rest on its base petal, perfectly positioned to roll the Sojourner rover down a ramp.

Sojourner was a 10.6 kg six-wheeled machine the size of a microwave oven, designed to last seven sols and instead working for 83. It drove about 100 m, performed chemical analyses with an alpha proton X-ray spectrometer, and photographed the surrounding rocks — including a rock nicknamed Yogi that helped establish that the plain was a flood deposit.

The landing site was named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station. Both vehicles are still in Ares Vallis; the lander's solar panels, mast and ramp are identifiable in later orbital images, making the site a small archaeological field of the first rover on Mars.

facts.label: Images
facts.value: More than 16,500 from the lander, 550 from the rover

sites.name: Mars Polar Lander crash site
sites.categoryDetail: Failed lander — likely engine shutdown too early
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Estimated impact area published by NASA GISS: about 76.1° S, 195.3° W (164.7° E). The spacecraft's exact resting place has not been located.
sites.summary: A polar lander that went silent minutes before touchdown, ending a bad year for Mars exploration.
narrative: Mars Polar Lander was meant to touch down near the south pole on 3 December 1999 and dig for ice. Instead it disappeared during the final descent. A review board concluded that the most likely cause was the premature shutdown of its descent engines: a sensor that detected the landing legs deploying was triggered by vibrations when the legs unfolded, so the engine controller believed touchdown had occurred high above the surface and cut the engines. The spacecraft fell the last 40 metres.

It carried two Deep Space 2 microprobes that were released during descent and were designed to smash into the surface and transmit from below ground. They were never heard from either. The failure, together with the loss of Mars Climate Orbiter the same year, led NASA to restructure its Mars programme and to adopt the more rigorous landing-system verification used for subsequent missions.
The wreckage has never been found in orbital images. Somewhere in the southern polar terrain there is a lander, a parachute, a backshell and two small penetrators, sitting where they fell.

sites.name: Beagle 2
sites.categoryDetail: Lander — landed intact but never deployed
sites.status: Silent — found intact in 2015 orbital images
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Position from Bridges et al. (2017) via NASA GISS; identified in HiRISE images about 5 km from the target centre.
sites.summary: Britain's Mars lander disappeared on Christmas Day 2003 — and was found eleven years later, apparently intact but unable to open.
narrative: Beagle 2 was a small British-built lander carried by ESA's Mars Express, designed to search for signs of life and to test a novel lightweight entry system. It separated from the orbiter on 19 December 2003 and was due to land on 25 December in Isidis Planitia. No signal was ever received, and the mission was declared lost in February 2004.

In January 2015 the HiRISE camera on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter found the lander in images taken in 2005. It was sitting close to its target, apparently upright, with its parachute and backshell nearby — the entry and descent had worked. What had failed was the deployment: at least two of its four solar-panel petals had not opened, so its antenna was never exposed to Earth.
Beagle 2 is a rare example of a lost lander found. It lies in Isidis Planitia partly unfolded, a spacecraft that reached Mars and then waited, in silence, to be noticed.

sites.name: Spirit — Columbia Memorial Station
sites.categoryDetail: Rover — six years in Gusev, finally stuck
sites.status: Mission ended 22 March 2010 — rover remains in place
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Landing site fix from the rover navigation solution (Li et al.), published by NASA GISS. The rover stopped in soft soil at a site called Troy, a few kilometres from the landing point; the marker shows the landing site.
sites.summary: A rover designed for 90 days that ran for six years, climbed mountains, and finally sank into a patch of soft sand.
narrative: Spirit landed inside Gusev Crater on 4 January 2004, bouncing to a stop inside airbags. Its twin Opportunity arrived three weeks later on the other side of the planet. Both were designed for 90 sols; both would last years.

Spirit's first year was difficult — it had to drive to features that showed evidence of water, and the crater floor was a plain of volcanic rock. It eventually found what it was looking for in the Columbia Hills: rocks that had been altered by water, and near- pure silica deposits that suggested hot springs. It climbed Husband Hill and reached the summit of a ridge in 2005, then descended to the edge of a small crater.

In May 2009 its wheels broke through a crust into soft sulphate sand near a feature called Troy. It took months to get out and never did, and with its solar panels badly angled for the Martian winter it lost power and stopped transmitting on 22 March 2010. NASA declared the mission over in May 2011. The rover is still at Troy, partially buried, tilted in the sand at the foot of a slope.

facts.value: Troy, soft sulphate sand, west of Home Plate

sites.name: Opportunity — Challenger Memorial Station
sites.categoryDetail: Rover — 45 km and 14 years, stopped by a global dust storm
sites.status: Mission ended 13 February 2019 — rover remains in Perseverance Valley
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Landing site fix from the rover navigation solution (Li et al.), published by NASA GISS; 354.47° E = 5.53° W. The rover's final position is about 45 km away at the rim of Endeavour crater; the marker shows the landing site.
sites.summary: The rover that drove a marathon on Mars, found the first clear evidence of ancient water, and went silent in a dust storm after 14 years.
narrative: Opportunity landed on Meridiani Planum on 25 January 2004 and almost immediately found what it came for. Within weeks it was examining sedimentary rocks with haematite concretions — the famous blueberries — and sulphate-rich layers that could only have formed in liquid water. The case for a wet early Mars, argued for decades, was settled by a rover that had been built to last three months.

It kept going for 14 years and 45.16 km, the longest drive on another world at the time. It descended into Endurance crater, survived a dust storm that nearly ended it in 2007, crawled out of Victoria crater, and finally reached the rim of the much older Endeavour crater, where it found gypsum veins deposited by water flowing through rock.

In June 2018 a planet-wide dust storm darkened the sky and Opportunity's solar panels could not keep its batteries charged. It sent a final transmission on 10 June 2018, then went silent. Engineers sent hundreds of recovery commands over eight months; the last went unanswered, and the mission was declared over on 13 February 2019. The rover is parked in Perseverance Valley on the western rim of Endeavour crater, its solar panels dusty, its tracks still visible from orbit.

sites.name: Phoenix Lander
sites.categoryDetail: Stationary lander — polar water ice
sites.status: Mission ended 2 November 2008 — lander remains, likely damaged by ice
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Landing fix provided by D. Bass, published by NASA GISS; 234.25° E = 125.75° W.
sites.summary: A lander that dug into the Martian arctic and touched water ice, then was buried by the winter.
narrative: Phoenix landed on 25 May 2008 at 68° N, well inside the Martian Arctic Circle, using the same airbag-and-retrorocket descent as the 1999 Mars Polar Lander but with a proven system. Its robotic arm dug trenches in the bright northern soil and, within weeks, exposed a white layer that disappeared over several days — water ice sublimating into the dry air.

The mission confirmed that ice lies just below the surface across the northern plains, measured an alkaline soil chemistry with perchlorate salts, and photographed falling snow above the landing site with a laser instrument. It also found calcium carbonate, evidence of a past atmosphere that could have supported liquid water.

As autumn approached, the Sun set for the winter and Phoenix stopped transmitting on 2 November 2008. Orbital images taken the following spring show that its solar panels appear to have been broken off by the weight of carbon-dioxide frost — the lander's own instruments told us the ice would do that, and the ice demonstrated it.

facts.value: Water ice confirmed centimetres below the surface

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Solar panels apparently broken by winter frost

sites.name: Curiosity — Bradbury Landing
sites.categoryDetail: Rover — sky-crane landing, still operating
sites.status: Active — rover still exploring Gale Crater
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Landing fix provided by A. Vasavada, B. Semenov and J. Crisp, published by NASA GISS. The rover has since driven more than 30 km up the slopes of Mount Sharp.
sites.summary: A nuclear-powered laboratory that landed with a rocket-powered crane and proved Gale Crater once held a lake.
narrative: Curiosity arrived on 6 August 2012 using a descent sequence that had never been tried: a heat shield, a parachute, and then a rocket-powered sky crane that lowered the rover on cables and flew away to crash. The landing site was named Bradbury Landing after the author Ray Bradbury, who had died that June.

Within months the rover had found what the mission was sent for. Drilling into a mudstone at Yellowknife Bay revealed clay minerals, a freshwater lake environment and the chemical ingredients needed for microbial life — a habitable environment, though not evidence of life itself. Since then it has driven up the lower slopes of Mount Sharp, measuring how the ancient lake and groundwater changed as the planet dried.

Curiosity is powered by a plutonium radioisotope generator, so dust does not matter to it. It has now been operating for more than a decade, has climbed through metres of layered sedimentary rock, and has photographed solar eclipses by Phobos and the Earth in the Martian sky. It is a working laboratory the size of a car, still moving across the floor of Gale Crater.

facts.label: Key result
facts.value: Ancient freshwater lake and habitable conditions at Yellowknife Bay

sites.name: Schiaparelli crash site
sites.categoryDetail: Failed lander — parachute and retrorockets released early
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Impact point published by NASA GISS: 2.07° S, 353.79° E = 6.21° W; imaged by HiRISE about 5.5 km west of the planned target.
sites.summary: A European test lander that fell the last few kilometres after its parachute released too early, leaving a fresh crater in Meridiani.
narrative: Schiaparelli was ESA's entry, descent and landing demonstrator, built to prove European technology for the ExoMars rover. It entered the Martian atmosphere on 19 October 2016 and performed most of the descent correctly, but a sensor gave a false reading that indicated it was below ground level, so the computer jettisoned the parachute and fired the retrorockets far too early.

The engines burned for a few seconds and cut out. Schiaparelli fell about 3.7 km and struck the surface at more than 500 km/h, leaving a crater and a scatter of debris that was imaged by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter days later. The data it transmitted during descent, and the wreckage itself, provided the evidence needed to fix the software fault.

The site is only a few tens of kilometres from Opportunity's landing site in Meridiani Planum — two spacecraft from different eras and different agencies, within sight of each other's regions, one still driving and one destroyed on impact.

sites.name: InSight Lander
sites.categoryDetail: Stationary lander — seismology and interior structure
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Landing fix provided by B. Semenov, published by NASA GISS.
sites.summary: The first mission to listen to Mars — it recorded more than a thousand marsquakes and mapped the planet's interior.
narrative: InSight landed on Elysium Planitia on 26 November 2018 and deployed a seismometer onto the surface with a robotic arm, the first instrument of its kind placed directly on another planet. Over four years it detected more than 1,300 marsquakes, including a magnitude 5 event and a large impact that produced a fresh crater.

The seismic data let scientists measure the thickness of the Martian crust, the size of its core and the structure of its mantle — the first direct look at the interior of another rocky planet. A heat probe designed to hammer itself five metres down never got below the surface; the soil's friction was different from anything the team had modelled.

Dust accumulated on the solar panels until the lander produced 5% of its original power. It sent a final image and a last message in December 2022 and was declared finished on 21 December. Its site is one of the best-characterised patches of Mars: a flat plain, a seismometer, a heat probe stuck at the surface, and a lander covered in dust.

facts.value: SEIS seismometer, HP3 heat probe, RISE radio science

sites.name: Perseverance — Octavia E. Butler Landing
sites.categoryDetail: Rover — sample caching and the first powered flight on another planet
sites.status: Active — caching samples for a future return mission
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Landing fix published by NASA GISS (site known as Octavia E. Butler Landing). The rover has since driven to the crater rim; the marker shows the landing site.
sites.summary: A rover collecting Mars rocks for a future trip to Earth, delivered with a helicopter that flew 72 times on another world.
narrative: Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater on 18 February 2021, in a dried-up lake bed with a river delta on one side. Its primary mission is sample caching: it drills cores from rocks and seals them in titanium tubes, leaving them on the surface for a future mission to collect and return to Earth. Those samples are the first deliberately prepared for interplanetary delivery from another planet.

It also carried Ingenuity, a 1.8 kg helicopter with counter-rotating blades built to fly in an atmosphere 1% as thick as Earth's. Planned as a five-flight technology demonstration, it made 72 flights over nearly three years, scouting terrain and ending its mission in January 2024 after a rotor was damaged on landing.

The rover has since explored the delta front, found evidence for organic molecules and lake sediments, and begun climbing the western rim of Jezero. Its microphones have recorded Martian wind and the sound of its own wheels on rock — the first sounds from another planet.

sites.name: Zhurong rover
sites.categoryDetail: Rover — dormant since 2022
sites.status: Hibernating since May 2022; contact not re-established
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric areographic, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Landing coordinates published by NASA GISS (from CNSA/Tianwen-1 data). The rover drove about 1.9 km from the landing platform.
sites.summary: China's first Mars rover drove nearly two kilometres, found evidence of water-altered ground, and went quiet in the Martian winter.
narrative: Zhurong landed in southern Utopia Planitia on 15 May 2021 as part of China's Tianwen-1 mission and rolled off its lander platform a week later. It carried a ground-penetrating radar, a magnetic field detector, a weather station and cameras, and over 358 sols it drove about 1.9 km.

The radar found layered structures beneath the surface consistent with buried sediments and possibly ancient water activity; the rover also found hydrated minerals in the soil. In May 2022 it entered hibernation for the northern winter, expecting to wake when temperatures rose. It never answered, probably because dust on its solar panels prevented it from generating power.

Orbital images from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showed the rover stationary for months before the Chinese team confirmed the loss. Its landing platform, ramp and the rover itself remain on the plain, the first Chinese hardware on another planet.

sites.categoryDetail: Impactor — first human object to reach the Moon
sites.coordSystem: Mean Earth/Polar Axis lunar frame, planetocentric (DE421)

sites.summary: The first human-made object to touch another world — a sphere of instruments and pentagonal pennants, fired into the Moon in 1959.
narrative: Luna 2 left Earth on 12 September 1959 carrying a package of Soviet pennants, and struck the Moon on 13 September. It was the first time any human-built object had reached another celestial body, and the event was reported as a triumph: the spacecraft's last transmission stopped exactly when predicted, confirming the impact.

The exact crater has never been identified, because the impact point was only known to within a couple of degrees and the region is covered with older craters. The Soviet Union claimed the impact within the Palus Putredinis; later analysis suggests somewhere in the Imbrium basin. Unlike later missions, Luna 2 was never meant to survive — it had no braking system, and arrival and destruction were the same event.

sites.categoryDetail: Impactor — first US spacecraft to reach another body
sites.coordSystem: Mean Earth/Polar Axis lunar frame, planetocentric (DE421)
sites.coordNote: NSSDCA publishes 15.5 S, 130.7 W; the spacecraft was on the far side and the impact point has not been imaged.
sites.summary: America's first spacecraft to reach the Moon arrived dead, after a timer failure, and hit the far side.
narrative: Ranger 4 launched on 23 April 1962 and suffered a failure of its central computer and timer during the coast. Without the timer the spacecraft could not perform its midcourse correction or its terminal sequence, and it arrived at the Moon on 26 April 1962 with no power.

It impacted the far side at about 15.5° S, 130.7° W, becoming the first US spacecraft to reach another celestial body — but it returned nothing. The far side was still a place known only from Luna 3's grainy photographs, and this crash left no mark anyone could see for decades.

sites.name: Ranger 6 impact site
sites.categoryDetail: Impactor — camera failure
sites.coordSystem: Mean Earth/Polar Axis lunar frame, planetocentric (DE421)
sites.coordNote: Impact point identified in LROC imagery.
sites.summary: Everything worked except the cameras. Ranger 6 hit the Moon blind, six months before Ranger 7 would succeed.
narrative: Ranger 6 arrived at the Moon on 2 February 1964 with a functioning spacecraft and a dead camera system. Six television cameras were commanded on during the final approach, and none produced an image — the high-voltage supply had arced before launch and never worked in flight.

The spacecraft still impacted on target, proving the navigation and terminal guidance. Five months later Ranger 7 repeated the flight with fixed cameras and sent back the first American close-ups of the Moon. The Ranger 6 impact crater, imaged from orbit, is a marker for one of the most productive failures in planetary exploration.

sites.name: Ranger 7 impact site
sites.categoryDetail: Impactor — first US close-up images of the Moon
sites.coordSystem: Mean Earth/Polar Axis lunar frame, planetocentric (DE421)
sites.coordNote: Impact point confirmed in LROC imagery.
sites.summary: A kamikaze camera probe that sent back 4,308 photographs in its last 17 minutes of flight.
narrative: Ranger 7 was built to die taking pictures. On 31 July 1964 it fell towards Mare Cognitum with six television cameras running, transmitting the first close-up views of the lunar surface ever returned by a US spacecraft — 4,308 images in 17 minutes, ending with frames taken from a few hundred metres up.

The images were deliberately spread across the approach so engineers could see the surface at every scale, from continental to boulder. They showed that the maria were covered in small craters and that a lander would not simply sink into a dust sea, which had been a serious fear. The spacecraft hit at about 2.7 km/s; its crater has since been found in Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images.

sites.name: Ranger 8 impact site
sites.categoryDetail: Impactor — Apollo site reconnaissance
sites.coordSystem: Mean Earth/Polar Axis lunar frame, planetocentric (DE421)
sites.coordNote: Impact point confirmed in LROC imagery.
sites.summary: Ranger 8 photographed the future Apollo 11 landing region from above, then crashed into it.
narrative: Ranger 8 was aimed at the eastern Sea of Tranquility, the region NASA was already considering for the first crewed landing. It returned 7,137 photographs during its final 23 minutes, including frames at resolutions that let planners pick out boulders, slopes and small craters.

It impacted on 20 February 1965 at 2.6376° N, 24.7881° E, within about 30 km of where Apollo 11 would land four years later. The comparison between Ranger images and the Lunar Module's view on approach is one of the quiet through-lines of the programme: the site was surveyed by an impactor, and then visited by people.

sites.categoryDetail: Impactor — final Ranger

sites.summary: The last Ranger flew into Alphonsus crater, aiming at the dark halo deposits that some astronomers thought might be volcanic.
narrative: Ranger 9 targeted Alphonsus, a 119 km crater on the edge of Mare Nubium, because photographs from Earth showed dark haloes and rilles that might be volcanic vents. During its final 18 minutes it returned 5,814 images on live television, watched by an audience that included scientists hoping to see evidence of active geology.

The images showed craters, ridges and rubble but no unambiguous volcanic vents; the dark halo material turned out to be older, darker ejecta. Ranger 9 crashed at 12.8281° S, 2.3884° W, ending the programme with a live broadcast from a spacecraft falling into a crater.

sites.summary: The first spacecraft to land softly on the Moon and send pictures back from its surface — and we still do not know exactly where it sits.
narrative: Luna 9 fell through the lunar night to the surface on 3 February 1966, bounced and rolled inside inflated airbags, then opened four petals and raised a camera. It returned the first photographs ever taken from the surface of another world: a bleak plain of dust and small stones, a sky utterly black, the horizon close.

The Soviet Union published the coordinates as 7.13° N, 64.37° W, and for decades that was the record. When Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter began photographing the Moon in detail, no lander could be found there, and the shadows in the original images suggested the true latitude and longitude were wrong by kilometres. The craft is somewhere in the Oceanus Procellarum, still transmitting nothing, one of the most important machines in space history and one of the hardest to find.
It mattered less for what it found than for what it proved: that a spacecraft could survive a landing and that the surface would hold it. Four months later, NASA's Surveyor 1 followed it down.

It sent back more than 11,000 images over six weeks, including views of its own footpads to show how far they had sunk. That engineering data — bearing strength, slope, surface texture — is why the Apollo crews knew the regolith would support them. The lander is still there; LROC images show the bright triangle of its body and the dark shadow it casts.

On 23 August it turned a camera away from the Moon and took the first photograph of the Earth rising over the lunar horizon — an image that changed how people pictured their own planet.

The spacecraft carried limited propellant. To prevent its orbit from decaying unpredictably and to clear the way for later orbiters, controllers commanded a retro-fire and it struck the far side on 29 October 1966, at a spot later computed to about 6.35° N, 160.71° E. It was the first of five Lunar Orbiters to be deliberately disposed of this way.

narrative: Luna 13 landed on 24 December 1966 and deployed two folding arms fitted with penetrometers and a density gauge. By driving them into the surface, it measured the mechanical strength of the regolith — information that directly informed the design of lander legs, including those of the Apollo Lunar Module.

Its cameras returned several panoramas of a gently undulating plain strewn with rocks, taken at different times of day to show how the shadows changed. It was the last Soviet soft landing before the race moved to sample return and rovers, and its position in the Oceanus Procellarum has never been confirmed from orbit.

sites.summary: The only spacecraft on the Moon to be visited by humans — and the only one to have pieces of it brought home.
narrative: Surveyor 3 landed on 20 April 1967 on a gentle slope in Oceanus Procellarum. Two and a half years later, Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked up to it. They photographed the little lander, cut away its camera and scoop, and took samples of the soil around its footpads to see how the surface had weathered.

The returned hardware produced one of the strangest results of the Apollo programme: a colony of Streptococcus bacteria was found inside the camera housing, having survived two and a half years in vacuum and hard radiation. The finding was contentious and is still a cautionary tale in planetary protection — it showed how easily terrestrial microbes can hitch a ride, and how little we knew about their survival.

Surveyor 3 remains where Apollo 12 found it, with a pale thermal blanket and three footpads, its camera replaced by a hole. It is the only place in the solar system where two missions, three years apart, met by design.

sites.summary: A leaking helium tank nearly ended this mission in flight; it landed anyway and performed the first chemical analysis of another world's soil.
narrative: Surveyor 5 lost helium pressure during its coast to the Moon, which threatened the descent sequence. Engineers reprogrammed the landing to use radar and a lower-altitude braking start, and it set down in Mare Tranquillitatis on 11 September 1967.

It carried an alpha-scattering instrument that fired alpha particles into the soil and measured the energies of the returning particles. The result — a basaltic composition rich in iron and titanium — was the first chemical analysis performed on the surface of another world, and it matched the mare samples Apollo 11 would return two years later from almost the same region.
Surveyor 5 also photographed its own footpad sinking into the dust and returned 18,000 images during the first lunar night, when engineers were unsure whether it would survive the cold.

sites.summary: No rocket had ever lifted off from the Moon until this small lander did it, three times, and set itself back down.
narrative: Surveyor 6 was sent to Sinus Medii, near the centre of the Moon's visible disc. After three weeks of science it performed an experiment no spacecraft had attempted: its three small vernier engines were fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the lander about 3 to 4 metres off the surface and moving it roughly 2.5 metres sideways before it settled again.

The hop proved that a soft-landed spacecraft could take off from the Moon, a necessary demonstration for planning crewed ascent. It also gave engineers a second look at the same piece of ground from a slightly different angle, and left two landing marks — the original footprints of a 300-kilogram machine and the shallow divots of its second touchdown.

sites.summary: The last Surveyor landed in the bright, rugged highlands near Tycho — a different world from the flat mare sites it was built to study.
narrative: Surveyor 7 landed 29 km from the rim of Tycho on 10 January 1968, the only Surveyor sent to the lunar highlands. Its camera found a rougher, brighter surface than the mare sites had shown, with blocks of ejecta and a horizon of hills.

The alpha-scattering instrument measured a composition poorer in iron and titanium than the maria — the first hint of the distinction between mare basalt and highland anorthosite that Apollo would later confirm. One laser beam, aimed at Earth for a ranging experiment, was never detected, an early lesson in how hard it is to bounce light off a target the size of a desk 384,000 km away.
Surveyor 7 was the last of its programme; the next spacecraft to make a soft landing on the Moon would be Apollo 11.

sites.name: Tranquility Base — Lunar Module Eagle

sites.summary: The first place humans walked on another world. The lower half of Eagle is still standing in the dust, with a laser reflector that still answers telescopes on Earth.
narrative: At 20:17 UTC on 20 July 1969 the Lunar Module Eagle settled into the Sea of Tranquility with about 25 seconds of hover fuel left. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin had spent the last minutes of the descent flying manually past a boulder field that the automatic guidance was steering them into. When the contact light came on, Armstrong said the words the whole planet was waiting for: Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.

They stayed on the surface for 21 hours and 36 minutes. Armstrong stepped onto the dust at 02:56 UTC on 21 July and described it as very, very fine-grained, almost like a powder. The single moonwalk lasted two and a half hours, covered about 250 metres and returned 21.55 kilograms of rock and soil. The site was photographed far more thoroughly than it was explored — most of the hardware was left exactly where the checklist put it.

What remains is an archaeological layer rather than a wreck. The octagonal descent stage is the base of the site; the ascent stage carrying the crew back to Michael Collins in Columbia was jettisoned and its impact point was never located. Around the descent stage lie the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package, the Laser Ranging Retroreflector, a seismometer, a flag held out by a horizontal rod, a plaque reading Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, and the discarded backpacks, boots and cameras of two men who had to fit into a very small cabin to get home.

The retroreflector is the reason this site is not entirely silent. Apollo 11's mirror and the arrays left by Apollo 14 and 15 are still used by laser ranging stations, and measurements made against them tell us that the Moon is moving away from Earth at about 3.8 centimetres a year. Tranquility Base has been a UNESCO-style heritage site in everything but paperwork: LROC images show the bright speck of the descent stage, the dark smear of disturbed soil, and the thin trails of two pairs of boots.

sites.categoryDetail: Scientific instrument still in use
sites.status: Still operating — ranged by observatories worldwide

sites.coordNote: NSSDCA publishes the reflector position separately from the descent stage because it is a separate, precisely surveyed target.
sites.summary: A suitcase-sized array of 100 corner cubes that has been bouncing laser pulses back to Earth since 1969 — the only Apollo experiment still returning data.
narrative: Aldrin set the retroreflector down a short walk from Eagle and levelled it by hand. It has no power supply, no moving parts and no electronics: a hundred fused-silica corner cubes that send any incoming laser pulse straight back where it came from. Apollo 14 and Apollo 15 left larger arrays; the Soviet Lunokhod rovers left French-built ones. Together they form a passive geodesy network that needs no maintenance.

Observatories such as Apache Point in New Mexico fire short pulses at these arrays and count the photons that return. From the travel time they measure the Earth–Moon distance to millimetres, and from years of those measurements they have established that the Moon recedes by about 3.8 cm per year, that the lunar orbit's shape wobbles in ways that constrain its interior, and that Einstein's description of gravity still holds at this distance. When the Apollo programme ended, this small slab of glass kept working.

sites.summary: A Soviet sample-return attempt that crashed while Apollo 11 was on the surface — the most dramatic near-miss of the space race.
narrative: Luna 15 was launched three days before Apollo 11 and entered lunar orbit while Armstrong and Aldrin were on the surface. It was a sample-return attempt designed to bring back material ahead of the American crew, and it spent two days manoeuvring before beginning its descent on 21 July 1969.

The descent failed. Soviet sources later described the spacecraft striking the Moon in the Mare Crisium region at high speed; tracking and later reconstructions place it between 12° and 17° north, near 60° east, though no crater has been conclusively matched. British tracking stations listening to the mission, and reporting on it during the Apollo 11 landing, gave the world one of the more bizarre details of that week: a race that ended in a crater.

sites.summary: The first precision landing on the Moon — and the only time humans walked up to a spacecraft that had arrived three years earlier.
narrative: Apollo 12 launched into a rainstorm on 14 November 1969 and was struck by lightning twice during ascent, which knocked the fuel cells offline until mission control improvised a fix. Four days later Pete Conrad and Alan Bean set Intrepid down within about 180 metres of Surveyor 3, a robot that had landed in April 1967. It was the first time a crew had proved they could land somewhere specific rather than somewhere safe.

The second moonwalk was a walk to a museum object. Conrad and Bean cut pieces off Surveyor 3 — its television camera, a sample scoop, tubing — and brought them home, where engineers found terrestrial bacteria inside the camera housing. The site's two visits, three years apart, made it the first place where a machine was inspected by people. They also deployed the first complete Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package, which transmitted until its power source was switched off in September 1977.

The site is a compact field of hardware: the descent stage of Intrepid, the sprawling ALSEP station and its radioisotope generator, and the pale Surveyor 3 lander 180 m away with its three footpads and white thermal blanket. Two pairs of bootprints connect the three.

Rather than leave it in an unstable orbit, controllers fired its remaining propellant to send it back into the Moon at 1.68 km/s, about 73 km from the still-listening seismometer the crew had just deployed.

The impact produced a signal the lunar seismometers recorded clearly and became the first human-made calibration event on another world. narrative: Apollo 13's upper stage was always meant to be thrown at the Moon after separating from the spacecraft, both to dispose of it and to give the seismometers a calibrated impact. On 15 April 1970 it struck at 2.555° S, 27.8875° W with an energy of about 4.6 × 10¹⁷ erg, producing a signal recorded by the Apollo 12 station.

By then the crew were in a crippled command module, looping around the Moon on a free-return trajectory after an oxygen tank explosion. That impact signal, and the seismic data it produced, helped refine models of the lunar crust that were later used to understand the kind of terrain the abandoned mission had been aiming for. The site has been imaged from orbit: a fresh, bright crater with dark rays of ejecta.

The 101 grams it returned were the first lunar samples brought back by a machine, and they showed that Mare Fecunditatis basalt was older than the Apollo 11 material. The lander itself was never meant to move again. It sits beside the ramp marks with its instrument mast and dish still attached, one of the best-preserved Soviet landing sites on the Moon. The rover it released ended up a few kilometres away, and its position was recovered in 2010 when the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera spotted a bright glint — laser pulses from Earth confirmed it was the retroreflector carried on board.

sites.summary: The first rover on another world was lost for 39 years — then found because its mirror was still catching laser light.
narrative: Lunokhod 1 was driven by a team of five men in Crimea looking at television pictures with a two-second delay, a hard way to steer a vehicle with eight independently driven wheels. Over ten months it covered about 10.5 km and returned more than 20,000 images and hundreds of soil measurements. It was declared finished in October 1971, when its operators could no longer communicate with it.

For decades nobody knew exactly where it had stopped. In 2010 the LROC team found a small bright spot in Mare Imbrium, and laser ranging verified it: the rover's corner-cube reflector was still returning photons. That identification turned a lost machine into a precise geodetic station, and removed a long-standing puzzle — Lunokhod 1's reflector had been returning signals at times when it should have been in shadow, because its position was wrong by several kilometres.
The rover now sits in the dust with its lid, cameras and antennae, the last wheel tracks of a machine that explored the Moon before anyone drove a car there.

sites.summary: The landing that recovered the Apollo programme after Apollo 13 — Shepard and Mitchell hiked to Cone Crater and left a seismometer that detected meteoroid impacts for years.
narrative: Fra Mauro is what Apollo 13 would have explored. Apollo 14 arrived instead, on 5 February 1971, with Alan Shepard — America's first astronaut — and Edgar Mitchell on board. They set down in the hummocky ejecta blanket thrown out by the impact that formed Mare Imbrium, material that promised a window into the Moon's early history.

The navigation on this site was difficult. Their longest traverse, towards Cone Crater, ended in a slow climb across a landscape where every hummock looked like the next; they turned back short of the rim rather than risk the walk home. Their samples showed the site was not pristine Imbrium ejecta but a complex, layered terrain, and later analysis used them to date the basin-forming impact.

The hardware they left is the usual archaeology of an Apollo site: the descent stage of Antares, an ALSEP station with a seismometer, a laser reflector, and — famously — two golf balls hit with a makeshift club. The seismometer recorded the deliberate crash of the Apollo 14 S-IVB stage and continued to detect small impacts for years, showing that the Moon's crust rings like a bell.

Over three moonwalks — 19 hours outside, a record at the time — they drove 27.9 km, climbing the slope of Hadley Delta, sampling the green volcanic glass of the rille edge and collecting 77.31 kilograms of rock, including the anorthosite known as the Genesis Rock. The vehicle itself carried the crew, their tools, a colour television camera and a navigation system that told them where they were on a world without roads.

When they left, the rover was parked about 90 metres east of Falcon with its wheels turned, still holding the tools from the last traverse. It is visible from orbit, as is the descent stage, the ALSEP station, and the tracks that run from the landing site out to the rille and back.

Together, the crewed and robotic samples supported the idea that the early Moon was covered by a global magma ocean whose light crystals floated to the top.
