sites.summary: Sent to the lunar highlands to prove they were volcanic; the rocks said otherwise, and rewrote the Moon's early history.
narrative: Apollo 16 was aimed at the Descartes formation, a bright highland region that many geologists expected to be the product of ancient volcanism. John Young and Charles Duke landed there on 21 April 1972 and spent three days driving across the Cayley Plains and the Descartes Mountains, collecting 95.71 kilograms of rock.

Almost none of it was volcanic. The samples were breccias — smashed and re-melted rock fragments welded together by impacts — which pushed the interpretation of the highlands from volcanism to a history dominated by gigantic collisions. It is one of the clearest cases of a mission disproving its own hypothesis, and it changed how planetary scientists read the bright terrains of every rocky body.

They also drove the rover at 18 km/h across the plain, the fastest anyone has driven on another world, and left behind a rover parked near the descent stage, an ALSEP station, a laser reflector, and a small subsatellite that operated in lunar orbit until its orbit decayed in 1979.

sites.summary: The last time anyone walked on the Moon. Cernan and Schmitt drove 35 km, found orange soil, and left a plaque that says we shall return.
narrative: Apollo 17 was the only mission with a geologist on the crew. Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt landed the Challenger in the Taurus-Littrow valley on 11 December 1972, a deep slice through the highlands where dark volcanic material and bright landslide debris meet.

Over three moonwalks lasting a total of 22 hours they drove 35 kilometres — the longest traverses of the programme — setting up a network of experiments and sampling a puzzling patch of orange soil at Shorty crater, later shown to be tiny volcanic glass beads erupted in fire fountains billions of years ago. They returned 110.52 kilograms of rock, the largest haul of any Apollo mission, and the most diverse.

Last out of the hatch, Cernan left a plaque reading Here man completed his first exploration of the Moon, December 1972 A.D., may the spirit of peace in which we came be reflected in the lives of all mankind. Beside the rover the crew had earlier placed a small aluminium figurine and a plaque commemorating astronauts and cosmonauts who had died. The descent stage, the rover, the ALSEP and the flag are still in the valley; the ascent stage was deliberately crashed nearby, and its seismic signature was recorded by the network the crews had built.

The lander deployed its ramps, the rover rolled down a day later and spent four months exploring. Before Luna 21's mission, no vehicle had crossed from mare basalt to highland crust in one journey. The descent stage and ramps still sit on the crater floor, visible from orbit.

In four months it covered about 42 km across the floor and rim of Le Monnier, photographing the edge of a crater and taking measurements of the boundary between mare and highland crust.

The end came from contamination, not wear. Dust settled on the radiators that kept the rover cool, and during the lunar day of May 1973 it overheated and lost pressure. Its last transmission was in June 1973. It still holds the distance record for a rover on the Moon, and its laser reflector is still used for ranging.
The rover is parked near the rim of Le Monnier with its lid open and its solar panel angled the way it was left, a Soviet machine that drove further on the Moon than any American rover has.

The core was important: it contained evidence of water-bearing minerals and showed the mare basalt here had a unusual titanium-rich composition. But its greater significance is historical. For 44 years the site sat alone, with no new visitors. The descent stage and the drilling equipment are still there, and the ascent stage's blast scar was photographed from orbit when the Moon was mapped again.

When its mission ended, engineers aimed it into Shoemaker crater near the south pole, hoping the impact might liberate detectable water vapour.

The spacecraft carried a small capsule containing the ashes of Eugene Shoemaker, the geologist who had trained the Apollo astronauts and who had spent his career studying impact craters. The plume rose about 1.6 km above the crater floor. Spectra from the shepherding spacecraft showed water vapour and ice, along with hydrogen, carbon monoxide, mercury and other volatiles — enough water in the excavated material to suggest that polar cold traps hold significant deposits. sites.summary: The first landing on the far side of the Moon, inside the oldest and largest impact basin in the solar system.
narrative: Chang'e 4 landed on 3 January 2019 inside Von Kármán crater, in the South Pole–Aitken basin — the far side of the Moon, which never faces Earth and had never been landed on. Because direct radio contact is impossible, the mission relies on a relay satellite at the Earth–Moon L2 point.

The Yutu-2 rover has since driven several hundred metres, finding material from the lunar mantle mixed into the regolith and measuring a strange gel-like substance in a small crater. The landing site sits in the deepest impact structure known on the Moon, and the rover's ground-penetrating radar has mapped its buried layers.
The lander and rover are the newest long-lived machines on the lunar surface, and they are alone on the side of the Moon that no one has ever seen from the ground.

facts.value: First soft landing on the lunar far side

sites.coordNote: Impact crater identified by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera, roughly 400 km from the intended landing site.
sites.summary: Russia's first lunar mission in 47 years spun out of control during a pre-landing burn and left a fresh crater in the south.
narrative: Luna 25 arrived in lunar orbit on 16 August 2023, the first Russian mission to the Moon since Luna 24 in 1976. On 19 August, during a manoeuvre to lower its orbit before a planned landing near the south pole, an engine burn lasted too long and the spacecraft was lost.

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter found the impact point within days: a fresh crater about 10 m across at 57.865° S, 61.36° E. Its arrival and destruction repeated, in a modern way, the pattern of the early lunar programme: missions that fail are still visible on the surface, and still part of the record.

sites.summary: India became the fourth country to land on the Moon, and the first to do it near the south pole.
narrative: Chandrayaan-3 landed on 23 August 2023 at about 69° S, making India the fourth nation to achieve a soft lunar landing and the first to touch down in the high southern latitudes now targeted by every major space programme. The Vikram lander deployed the six-wheeled Pragyan rover, which drove across the regolith measuring composition and temperature.

The mission confirmed the presence of sulphur, aluminium, iron and other elements near the surface, measured a steep thermal gradient in the soil, and detected a possible seismic event. The lander includes a NASA passive laser retroreflector array that is still usable for ranging.

After the two-week lunar day both vehicles went into sleep mode for the night. India woke them; they did not respond. Vikram and Pragyan remain on the surface at a site India has named Shiv Shakti Point.

sites.coordNote: Landing site identified in LROC images; the lander is roughly 80° S, 1.44° E.
sites.summary: The first privately built spacecraft to land on the Moon arrived safely and fell over — the first US soft landing since 1972.
narrative: Odysseus, built by Intuitive Machines for NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme, landed near Malapert A on 22 February 2024. It was the first American spacecraft to land softly on the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972, and the first commercial landing in history.

During descent its laser rangefinders failed, and the team improvised using an experimental NASA navigation payload that happened to be on board. The lander came down faster than planned, broke a leg, and tipped onto its side. Several antennas pointed the wrong way, but enough science data was returned in seven days — including images of the landing site and the eclipse of the Sun by the Earth — to make the mission a qualified success.

The site is a few degrees from the south pole, in terrain that will be visited by crewed Artemis missions. Odysseus is now a tilted monument on a slope, one of the first commercial artefacts on another world.

sites.summary: A commercial lander that arrived upright, survived a lunar night's worth of science, and photographed a total eclipse of the Sun by the Earth.
narrative: Blue Ghost Mission 1, built by Firefly Aerospace for NASA's CLPS programme, landed in Mare Crisium on 2 March 2025 — the first commercial mission to touch down upright and complete its full planned surface operations. It carried ten NASA payloads, including a regolith vacuum, a thermal probe, a navigation experiment and a stereo camera.

Over two weeks of daylight it drilled and sampled the surface, measured heat flow, and captured the first high-definition images of the lunar horizon and of a total solar eclipse seen from the Moon, when the Earth passed in front of the Sun on 14 March. It shut down at sunset as planned, having returned 119 gigabytes of data.
The lander now sits in the mare with its legs, solar panels and instruments, a new kind of object in the lunar record: a commercially built machine rather than a national one.

sites.summary: A commercial lander carrying a NASA drill and a hopping robot came down inside a cold crater and fell on its side.
narrative: Athena was the second Intuitive Machines lander, carrying NASA instruments including a regolith drill, a mass spectrometer and a small hopping robot called Micro-Nova designed to drop into a permanently shadowed crater. It touched down near Mons Mouton on 6 March 2025, much closer to the pole than planned.

Its navigation put it down on a slope inside a small crater; it tipped over and could not complete its science sequence. Ground teams ran a reduced mission for a few hours before the lander lost power. The site is in the region being surveyed for Artemis — a place where NASA is learning, through hardware on the ground, how hard the polar terrain is to land on.

sites.name: Pioneer Venus Large Probe impact site
sites.categoryDetail: Atmospheric probe — crushed on impact
sites.status: Transmitted for 54 minutes during descent; destroyed on impact
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric Venus coordinates, east longitude
sites.coordNote: Entry and impact point published by NSSDCA: 4.4° N, 304.0° E = 56.0° W. Position derived from tracking; the impact itself was not observed.
sites.summary: A one-and-a-half metre sphere that fell through the Venusian clouds for 54 minutes before the surface crushed it.
narrative: On 9 December 1978 the Pioneer Venus Multiprobe released four descent vehicles into the atmosphere of Venus. The largest was a 1.5 m sphere inside a protective aeroshell, carrying seven instruments to measure the atmosphere's composition, clouds, radiation and pressure from the top of the cloud deck down to the surface.

It entered at 11.5 km/s on the night side, deployed a parachute at 47 km, and transmitted for 54 minutes as it descended. At the surface, where the temperature is about 465 °C and the pressure 92 times Earth's, the probe stopped transmitting immediately on impact — its internal electronics had been kept cool by a small heat sink for exactly this long, and no more.

The four probes and their bus reached Venus within seven minutes of each other, spread over the planet. The coordinates of each impact point are known only from tracking and atmospheric models, and Venus's permanent clouds mean nobody has ever seen the ground where they landed.

facts.value: 7, including mass spectrometer and gas chromatograph

sites.name: Pioneer Venus Day Probe — the survivor
sites.categoryDetail: Atmospheric probe — survived impact for 67 minutes
sites.status: Survived impact and transmitted for 67 minutes from the surface
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric Venus coordinates, east longitude
sites.coordNote: NSSDCA: 31.3° S, 317.0° E = 43.0° W. Derived from tracking; the probe's final resting place has never been imaged.
sites.summary: The only spacecraft to keep transmitting from the surface of Venus — one hour and seven minutes of data from the most hostile place we have ever landed.
narrative: Three of the four Pioneer Venus probes died at the moment they hit the surface. The small Day probe did not. Its aeroshell had been designed without a parachute to fall fast, and it was built a little more robustly; after landing it continued to transmit for 67 minutes, measuring the temperature and pressure of the air around it as it slowly cooked.

That hour is the longest any spacecraft has operated on the surface of Venus. The data confirmed the astonishing conditions at the surface — about 465 °C, pressure equivalent to being 900 m under the ocean — and showed that the atmosphere near the ground was calmer than expected.

The probe itself is a crushed sphere somewhere in the lowlands, its antenna still pointed at a sky it cannot see through. Venus has no visible surface from orbit, so the exact site will probably never be photographed.

sites.categoryDetail: Atmospheric probe — destroyed on impact
sites.status: Transmitted during descent; destroyed on impact
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric Venus coordinates, east longitude
sites.coordNote: NSSDCA: 59.3° N, 4.8° E, from tracking and entry reconstruction.
sites.summary: A small probe sent into the northern day-side atmosphere, which survived the fall and not the landing.
narrative: The North probe was targeted at 60° N on the day side of Venus, where the Sun is high and the atmosphere is at its most vigorously convective. It entered the atmosphere without a parachute, protected only by an aeroshell, and transmitted temperature, pressure and cloud data as it fell.

It struck the surface at about 19:42 UTC and stopped transmitting immediately. Its measurements, combined with those from the other three probes, showed how Venus's atmosphere circulates: super-rotating winds at the cloud tops, a slow descent, and a surface almost entirely without wind.

The probe's impact point is known only from tracking, in a landscape no camera has seen. Venus's clouds are permanent, so every surface feature on this globe is inferred from radar rather than observed.

sites.categoryDetail: Atmospheric probe — destroyed on impact
sites.status: Transmitted during descent; destroyed on impact
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric Venus coordinates, east longitude
sites.coordNote: NSSDCA: 28.7° S, 56.7° E, from tracking and entry reconstruction.
sites.summary: The probe that fell into the Venusian night, where the clouds are thickest and the surface never sees the Sun.
narrative: The Night probe entered on the dark side of Venus at about 19:56 UTC and transmitted for just under an hour before hitting the surface at 19:52 local entry time — a fall through 200 km of atmosphere in roughly 55 minutes.

Its instruments measured the temperature profile and the net radiation balance in the deep atmosphere, where the greenhouse effect is so extreme that the ground is hotter than the day-side surface. It stopped transmitting two seconds after impact, as designed — the electronics had a fixed thermal budget and no way to survive beyond it.

All four probes were built to be destroyed, and all four were. The bus that carried them lasted slightly longer, burning up at about 110 km altitude, and the only thing that remains of the mission on Venus is four small crushed spheres that no instrument has ever seen.

sites.name: Pioneer Venus Multiprobe bus — burn-up point
sites.categoryDetail: Spacecraft bus — destroyed in the atmosphere
sites.status: Burned up at about 110 km altitude
sites.coordSystem: IAU planetocentric Venus coordinates, east longitude
sites.coordNote: NSSDCA gives the last tracked position as about 37.9° S, 290.9° E = 69.1° W, at 110 km altitude. There was no impact — the bus was destroyed in the atmosphere.
sites.summary: The carrier that released four probes into Venus lasted 25 minutes longer, then burned up without a heat shield.
narrative: The Pioneer Venus Multiprobe bus was a 2.5 m cylinder carrying one large and three small probes. It released them on 16 and 20 November 1978 and then flew into the atmosphere itself, with no heat shield and no parachute, transmitting measurements of the upper atmosphere that the probes could not make.

It survived to an altitude of about 110 km before the aerodynamic heating and pressure destroyed it, 25 minutes after the probes had gone in. It was the only part of the mission to sample the high atmosphere directly, and its last position is a point in the sky rather than a place on the ground.

This record exists in the archive because the bus was a spacecraft that ended at Venus, and because its fate — destroyed in flight — is the most common ending for the machines we send to other worlds.

facts.value: 9 December 1978, about 20:22 UTC, at roughly 110 km altitude
